$comment: This package's OWN emulator configuration, for the partner's project. It is not the repo-root
firebase.json, which configures the emulator kix-avvik's own partner store is tested against.
WHAT THE SEPARATION IS FOR, at the strength it was measured at. CI runs the two emulator steps
SEQUENTIALLY, and there the separation is what keeps a step clean when the previous one has not
finished tearing down -- observed on this machine, a Firestore emulator left holding 8572 for
minutes after its runner exited, and the next run then failed with `Port 8572 is not open`. It
is also what lets a developer run this suite while a repo-root emulator is already up: measured
6 of 6 runs clean, exit 0, 23/23, with the root suite live throughout.
WHAT IT IS NOT FOR, stated because the earlier version of this comment claimed it and was wrong.
It does NOT make two emulator suites safe to START AT THE SAME INSTANT. Measured 3 of 3 rounds:
the Firebase CLI prints its generic `Error: An unexpected error has occurred.` before running the
wrapped script, `emulators:exec` exits 2, and its error-path teardown can kill the script
mid-run. A probe found the hub listening on 4401 for 6 samples out of 40. The contention is
inside firebase-tools' own emulator hub startup, not in any port this file can name -- all three
nameable ports are separated below and the project id differs. Start one, wait for it to listen,
then start the other.
THE THREE PORTS, and two of them are invisible in the root config:
* firestore.port          8571 -> 8572
* hub.port                4400 (the CLI default; the root file does not name it) -> 4401
* firestore.websocketPort 9150 -> 9151. NOT covered by `firestore.port`: the CLI allocates it
separately, defaults it to 9150 for every project, and shifts it only by probing for a free
port at start-up -- a race two simultaneous starts both win. Pinning it makes the separation
deterministic instead of probabilistic.
And the emulator runs under its OWN demo project id (`demo-kixpartner`, in package.json's
test:emulator script). The CLI keys its hub locator file on the project id and warns that two
instances of one project `may result in unexpected behavior`; a distinct id answers that warning
rather than tolerating it. The suites read the id from GCLOUD_PROJECT, which `emulators:exec
--project` exports, so the two cannot disagree. Note a distinct id does NOT give a distinct
database: the emulator runs in --single_project_mode, which is why the two test files must run
serially (`--test-concurrency=1`).
`firestore.rules` must be named here or `emulators:exec` loads no rules and every deny assertion
in test/emulator/rules.test.mjs would pass against an open database.
